—If she says that, she shows good feeling, and it is honorable of her. But in telling you that, Germain, she does not cure you at all, for no doubt she tells you that she loves you and would marry you if we wished it?

—That is the worst of it! She says that her heart is not drawn to me.

—If she says what she does not think, in order to distance you from her more effectively, she is a child who deserves to be loved by us, and whose youth we should overlook because of her great good sense.

—Yes, said Germain, struck by a hope he had not yet conceived: that would be very wise and very _proper_ of her! But if she is so reasonable, I greatly fear it is because I displease her.

—Germain, said Mother Maurice, you are going to promise me to keep calm throughout the week, not to torment yourself, to eat, to sleep, and to be cheerful as you used to be. I shall speak to my old man, and if I persuade him to agree, you will then learn the girl’s true feelings toward you.

Germain promised, and the week passed without Father Maurice saying a word to him in private or appearing to suspect anything. The plowman strove to appear calm, but he kept growing paler and more tormented.


XVII


LITTLE MARIE


At last, on Sunday morning, as they came out of Mass, his mother-in-law asked him what he had obtained from his sweetheart since the conversation in the orchard.

—Why, nothing at all, he replied. I have not spoken to her.

—Then how do you expect to persuade her if you do not speak to her?

—I have spoken to her only once, Germain replied. That was when we went to Fourche together; and since that time I have not said a single word to her. Her refusal caused me so much pain that I would rather not hear her begin again to tell me that she does not love me.

—Well, my son, you must speak to her now; your father-in-law gives you leave to do so. Go, make up your mind! I am telling you to do it, and, if need be, I will it; for you cannot remain in such uncertainty.

Germain obeyed. He arrived at Guillette’s house with his head bowed and a crushed look upon his face. Little Marie was alone by the fire, so deep in thought that she did not hear Germain coming. When she saw him before her, she started in surprise upon her chair and turned bright red.

—Little Marie, he said to her as he sat down beside her, I have come to cause thee pain and trouble thee, and I know it well; but _the man and the woman of our house_ (thus designating, according to custom, the heads of the family) want me to speak to thee and ask thee to marry me. Thou dost not wish it; I expect as much.

—Germain, Little Marie replied, is it settled, then, that you love me?

—It vexes thee, I know, but it is not my fault: if thou couldst change thy mind, I should be only too happy, and no doubt I do not deserve that. Come, look at me, Marie; am I truly so hideous?

—No, Germain, she replied with a smile, you are handsomer than I am.

—Do not mock me; look at me indulgently; I have not yet lost a single hair or a single tooth. My eyes tell thee that I love thee. Look into my eyes, then; it is written there, and every girl knows how to read that writing.

Marie looked into Germain’s eyes with her playful assurance; then, all at once, she turned her head away and began to tremble.

—Ah, my God! I frighten thee, said Germain; thou lookest at me as if I were the farmer of Ormeaux. Do not fear me, I beg thee; it hurts me too much. I shall not say wicked things to thee; I shall not kiss thee against thy will, and when thou wishest me to go away, thou needst only show me the door. Come, must I leave so that thou wilt stop trembling?

Marie held out her hand to the plowman, but without turning her head away from the hearth toward which it was bowed, and without saying a word.

—I understand, said Germain; thou pitiest me, because thou art good; thou art sorry to make me unhappy: but still, thou canst not love me?

—Why do you say such things to me, Germain? Little Marie replied at last. Do you mean to make me cry?

—Poor little girl, thou hast a good heart, I know; but thou dost not love me, and thou hidest thy face from me because thou art afraid to let me see thy displeasure and thy repugnance. And I do not even dare to clasp thy hand! In the woods, when my son was asleep and thou wert sleeping too, I almost kissed thee very gently. But I would have died of shame rather than ask it of thee, and I suffered as much that night as a man who was being burned over a slow fire. Since then I have dreamed of thee every night. Ah, how I kissed thee, Marie! But thou, all that while, wert sleeping without dreaming. And now, dost thou know what I think? It is that if thou wert to turn around and look at me with such eyes as I have for thee, and if thou wert to bring thy face close to mine, I believe I should fall dead from joy. And thou, thou thinkest that if such a thing happened to thee, thou wouldst die of anger and shame!

Germain spoke as though in a dream, without hearing what he was saying. Little Marie was still trembling; but as he was trembling even more, he no longer noticed it. All at once she turned around; she was bathed in tears and was looking at him reproachfully. The poor plowman believed this was the final blow and, without waiting for her judgment, rose to leave; but the young girl stopped him by putting both arms around him and, hiding her head against his breast:

—Ah, Germain, she said to him between sobs, have you truly not guessed that I love you?

Germain would have gone mad if his son, who was looking for him and came galloping into the cottage astride a stick, with his little sister riding pillion and whipping the imaginary steed with a willow switch, had not brought him back to himself. He lifted the boy in his arms and, placing him in those of his betrothed:

—There, he said to her, thou hast made more than one person happy by loving me!






APPENDIX


I


THE COUNTRY WEDDING


Here ends the story of Germain’s marriage, just as he told it to me himself, the shrewd plowman that he is! Forgive me, dear reader, for not having known how to translate it better for thee; for the ancient and artless language of the peasants of the region I _sing_ (as people used to say) truly requires translation. Those people speak too much French for us, and since Rabelais and Montaigne, the progress of the language has caused us to lose many old riches. So it is with all progress; we must resign ourselves to it. But it is still a pleasure to hear those picturesque idioms holding sway over the old soil of central France, all the more because they are the true expression of the calmly mocking and pleasantly voluble character of the people who use them. Touraine has preserved a certain precious number of patriarchal turns of phrase. But Touraine became greatly civilized with and after the Renaissance. It became covered with châteaux, roads, foreigners, and activity. Berry remained unchanged, and I believe that after Brittany and a few provinces in the far south of France, it is the most _preserved_ region to be found at the present time. Certain customs are so strange, so curious, that I hope to amuse thee for another moment, dear reader, if thou wilt permit me to recount a country wedding in detail—for example, Germain’s, which I had the pleasure of attending a few years ago.
